title: Mary Anning, fossil hunter
text:
Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small town on the south coast of England. The crumbling cliffs near her home were full of fossils: the remains of animals and plants that lived millions of years ago.

Mary’s father, Richard, made furniture for a living. In his spare time, he collected fossils from the beach and sold them to visitors. He often took Mary and her brother, Joseph, with him and taught them how to search the rocks.

When Mary was eleven, her father died, and the family was left with very little money. Selling fossils became one of the ways they could pay for food and rent. Mary searched the shore after storms, when fresh rock had fallen from the cliffs, even though this was dangerous work.

In 1811, Joseph found the skull of a strange creature. About a year later, Mary uncovered the rest of its skeleton. It was an ichthyosaur, a sea reptile with a long, narrow snout and flippers shaped like paddles. The discovery caused great excitement among scientists.

Mary kept searching. In 1823, she found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a reptile with a tiny head and an extremely long neck. Some experts were so surprised that they suspected it was a fake! Five years later, she found the remains of a flying reptile, the first of its kind ever discovered in Britain.

Although Mary knew more about fossils than many professors, she was not allowed to join the Geological Society of London, because women could not become members at that time. Scientists bought her fossils and wrote about them, but they rarely mentioned her name.

Mary Anning died in 1847. Today, she is remembered as one of the greatest fossil hunters in history. Her discoveries helped scientists to understand that many kinds of animals had lived on Earth long ago and had since died out.
